summary.text: In Japanese, 生 is used for life, living, and birth. Its graph depicts a sprout emerging above the ground; early Chinese inscriptions attest uses for childbirth and living things, without establishing which came first.

formation.text: 生 is pictographic: 屮 depicts a sprout, while 一 marks the ground beneath it. A later mark below the sprout developed into a horizontal stroke, making the lower part resemble 土; that resemblance does not establish 土 as an original component.

components.text: In this analysis of 生, 屮 depicts the sprout above the ground. No phonetic role is proposed for it.

In the early analysis of 生, 一 marks the ground beneath the sprout. A later mark below 屮 developed into a horizontal stroke, making the lower part resemble 土; 土 is not identified as the original component.

history.text: The selected oracle-bone-style and Western Zhou bronze-style renderings illustrate the sprout-over-ground analysis. The graphic account describes early bronze forms as retaining this structure and a mark beneath the sprout later developing into a horizontal stroke. The images are modern vector renderings, and no dated sequence of individual artifacts is supplied.
A historical dictionary describes plants emerging above soil and glosses 生 as “advance”; a later interpretation treats “advance” as an extended sense rather than the graphic core.

生 was also used as a whole graph to write 姓, “surname,” a different word. This is described as sound-based reuse, but the evidence does not establish an ancient sound match: modern Mandarin readings are shēng and xìng, while supplied Middle Chinese forms are sraeng and sjengH. An oracle-bone phrase is read 多生, though 多甥 is an alternative analysis.

uncertainties.text: The oracle-bone phrase 生月 has been read as “following month,” but “this month” and other interpretations have also been proposed. Its meaning and any connection to life or growth remain disputed.

Reported uses include childbirth, live or fresh animals, producing or occurring, lifespan, and living. The evidence does not date every use or establish a sequence of semantic developments among them.
A conservative form 𤯓 is mentioned, but its chronology, ancestry, and possible relation to graphic corruption are unresolved in this evidence.

senses.text: 生 is reported in an oracle-bone prayer for childbirth. Other early uses are also reported, so this does not establish childbirth as the character’s original or first lexical meaning.
生 is reported as an adjective describing live animals in oracle-bone inscriptions. Its priority relative to the childbirth use is not established.
One interpretation reads 生月 as “following month”; other readings are contested. This phrase does not establish a semantic development from plant growth.
Oracle-bone examples describe live or fresh animals, and historical phonology entries separately record “fresh, raw.” No chronology connecting this sense to the others is established.
Bronze-inscription examples are reported with the sense “occur” or “produce.” The evidence does not show when or how this use developed from other senses.
A bronze-inscription example is reported with the sense “lifespan.” No transition from the other attested senses is established.
A historical dictionary glosses 生 as “advance”; a later interpretation treats this as an extended sense. The evidence does not date this sense or show its development.

senses.period: Warring States manuscripts and later usage
senses.text: A Warring States manuscript uses 生 for living in opposition to dying. Later lexicographic evidence also records life and living, without establishing a complete development from earlier uses.

Japanese dictionary evidence records 生きる for living, with an attestation in 宇治拾遺物語 dated about 1221, and lists 生まれる among the graph’s readings. These Japanese word uses are documented separately from ancient Chinese graph history; no continuous path between them is established.
Japanese dictionaries list 生 in words such as 生活 and 生命 and give life and living among its senses. These records do not establish a dated semantic chain from ancient Chinese uses.

limitations.text: The inscription examples support several uses but do not establish priority or a securely dated development chain among birth, living, freshness, production, lifespan, advance, and life.
The proposed sprout-and-ground image does not by itself show that every recorded word meaning developed from plant growth.
The “following month” reading of 生月 is disputed and does not demonstrate a semantic transition from growth or life to month terminology.

Japanese dictionaries document readings and vocabulary, but the evidence gives no complete dated history for when 生 acquired each Japanese reading or how those readings became associated with the graph.

overview.text: In Japanese, 生 is used for life, living, and birth. Its graph depicts a sprout above the ground.

components.text: In this early analysis, 屮 depicts the sprout above the ground.
In this early analysis, 一 marks the ground beneath the sprout.

relationships.text: In this analysis of 生, 屮 depicts the sprout in the sprout-emerging-from-ground image.
In this analysis of early 生, 一 marks the ground beneath the depicted sprout.

生 is reported as the sound element in 姓. Current Mandarin readings are shēng and xìng; supplied Middle Chinese forms are sraeng and sjengH, and Old Chinese forms are *sreŋ and *seŋ-s. These comparisons do not by themselves establish the historical sound relation.

summary.text: 生 has the on-readings セイ and ショウ and kun-readings such as いきる and うまれる. The on-readings are borrowed readings; the kun-readings pair the graph with native Japanese words.

readings.text: セイ is an on-reading used in compounds for life and living.
ショウ is another on-reading, recorded as a Wu reading.
いきる is a kun-reading: a Japanese word associated with 生, with okurigana written after the kanji.
うまれる is a kun-reading associated with the Japanese word for being born.
